summary: Proposes a fragment-oriented solution for the real-time encapsulation part of an architecture for combining multi-link PPP with multiple classes of traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2686 lets urgent traffic interrupt a large packet on a slow PPP link. The PPP Multilink header has bits that were never used, and the memo turns them into a class number that says how urgent a fragment is. Each class is numbered on its own, so a small urgent fragment can be sent in the middle of a big slow one without either side losing track of the pieces.

questions: how does ppp multilink support real-time traffic
what is prefix elision in ppp
how many priority classes does multi-class ppp support
subtitle: Spare bits in the PPP Multilink header become a class number, so urgent real-time fragments can slip between pieces of big packets on slow links.

tldr.problem: On a slow link, one large packet blocks the link for as long as it takes to send. A 1500 byte packet on a 28.8 kbit/s modem line occupies the link for about 400 ms, which is far too long for a conversation. The existing PPP Multilink protocol can only let urgent traffic past once, between fragments of a long packet.
tldr.mechanism: The memo takes bits that Multilink leaves unused in its header and gives them a new meaning: a class number. Each class gets its own sequence number space and its own reassembly buffer, so several independent sets of fragments can be in flight at once and a high-priority class can interrupt a low-priority one.
tldr.outcome: Together with the ability to send a packet with no Multilink header at all, the scheme gives four levels of suspension with the short header and sixteen with the long one. Two new LCP options, Multilink Header Format and Prefix Elision, let the two ends agree on the format and on common bytes that can be left out of every fragment.

facts.label: Unused bits in the multilink header
facts.value: 2 in the short sequence number format, 6 in the long

facts.label: Header format codes
facts.value: 2 long sequence number with classes, 6 short sequence number with classes

facts.label: Blocking time for a 1500 byte packet
facts.value: About 400 ms on a 28.8 kbit/s modem link

facts.label: Default when nothing is negotiated
facts.value: Long sequence number headers with class 0 only

today: RFC 2686 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It is the fragment-oriented part of the architecture in RFC 2689; the suspend and resume alternative for senders of type 1 is RFC 2687.

sections.title: The Problem on a Slow Link
sections.content:
Besides the best-effort service the Internet is known for, integrated services that carry real-time multimedia information are being developed and deployed. This document defines the fragment-oriented solution for the real-time encapsulation part of the architecture described in its companion RFC 2689, which covers integrated services over low-bitrate links such as modem lines, ISDN B-channels and sub-T1 links. That architecture has a real-time encapsulation format, a header compression architecture, elements of negotiation protocols between routers, and announcement protocols that let applications start the negotiation.

A real-time encapsulation format is needed because of how long a big packet occupies a slow link. A 1500 byte packet on a 28.8 kbit/s modem link makes that link unavailable for real-time information for about 400 ms. That worst-case delay pushes the round-trip delay of a real-time application to at least a second, which is not acceptable for real-time conversation.

The extensions defined here let a sender fragment the packets of several priorities into multiple classes of fragments, so that a high-priority packet can be sent between the fragments of a lower-priority one. A companion document, RFC 2687, gives a suspend and resume solution for the cases where the best possible delay is required and the senders are of type 1 in the architecture's terms.
sections.plainLanguage: A big packet fills a slow link for as long as it takes to send it, and that time is far too long for a live conversation. The memo lets a sender split its traffic into priority classes so that a small urgent piece can be sent in the middle of a large slow one.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
The main design goal for a real-time architecture over low-bitrate links is minimising the end-to-end delay. More precisely, the worst case delay, after removing outliers that are equivalent to packet losses from an application's point of view, is what determines the playout points the applications choose and therefore the delay the user actually perceives. Every attempt should also be made to maximise the bandwidth actually available to media data, which means keeping overheads small. The solution should not put unnecessary burdens on non-real-time flows, and the usual MTU should stay available to them.

The memo then works out how many levels of priority are really needed. The most general approach would let any packet be suspended for a more urgent one, to an unlimited depth, but in practice it is unlikely that a real-time packet will ever have to suspend another real-time packet that is not at least about twice as long. The largest packet size to be expected on a PPP link is the default MTU of 1500 bytes, and the smallest high-priority packets are likely to be on the order of 22 bytes, as compressed RTP and G.723.1 packets are. Across that 1:72 range of sizes, the memo works out a maximum requirement of about eight levels of suspension, including one level where long real-time packets suspend long non-real-time packets. On 28.8 kbit/s modems, it says, there seems to be a practical requirement for at least two levels of suspension, so that audio suspends any longer packet including video, and video suspends other very long packets.

Five further requirements are set for the fragmentation scheme. It must be predictable enough for admission control to make decisions from its characteristics, which will often need extra hints about the flow from the application. It must be robust against errors, at least with the same level of error detection as PPP. It must cooperate with PPP, and be as compatible with existing PPP standards as possible: on a link that makes use of the scheme, it must always be possible to fall back to standard LCP without ambiguity. It must work with existing chips and router systems, which for synchronous links means HDLC framing, and with much existing hardware it is hard to switch off the per-frame CRC; for asynchronous links there is more freedom, but a design that treats them very differently would lose desirable properties of PPP. And it must be future proof, in particular because the emergence of V.80 based modems may change the way PPP is used with modems.

The memo does not address requirements that may be relevant in conjunction with Frame Relay, but notes there seems to be little problem in applying its principles to PPP in Frame Relay.
sections.plainLanguage: The design has to keep the worst-case delay small, keep overhead low, and leave ordinary traffic alone. Working from the sizes of packets that really occur, the memo concludes that about eight levels of priority are enough in general and two on a modem link, and it lists the properties the scheme must have, including that it must detect errors as well as PPP does and that it must fall back cleanly to plain PPP.

sections.title: Using PPP Multilink as It Is
sections.content:
Transmitting only part of a packet so that higher-priority traffic can intervene, and resuming the transmission later, is a kind of fragmentation. The existing PPP Multilink Protocol of RFC 1990 provides sequence numbering and begin and end bits, which allows packets to be split into fragments. In its short sequence number form the header carries the address and control octets, the protocol identifier, a begin bit, an end bit and a sequence number, followed by the fragment data and the PPP frame check sequence.

Multilink's sequence numbering is monotonic, and contiguous numbers are needed for all the fragments of one packet, so it does not allow a run of fragments of one packet to be suspended in order to send another packet. It is, however, possible to send intervening packets that carry no multilink header at all, so multilink as it is supports two levels of priority.

The memo notes that this approach can be built from existing standards. Multilink capability is widely deployed, and only the sending side needs to know it is being used to give priority to real-time packets.

Two limitations are named. Because of the single monotonic serial number there is only one level of suspension: big packets sent through multilink can be suspended by small packets sent outside multilink, and those small packets are not fragmentable, so the content of one packet cannot be sent in parallel on several links, and if packets are sent in rounds on several links the order they are processed at the receiver may differ from the order they were sent. The second limitation is not solved by this specification either: the multilink header is relatively large, and as delay bounds become small for queues-of-fragments implementations that overhead may become significant.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain PPP Multilink can already split a packet and let a small packet slip between the pieces, but only one level of priority is possible, because all the pieces share one number series. The memo uses that as its starting point.

sections.title: Extending Multilink to Multiple Classes
sections.content:
The obvious way to get more than one level of suspension is to run Multilink several times over one link, but Multilink as defined provides no way for more than one instance to be active. Fortunately a number of bits are unused in the Multilink header: two in the short sequence number format and six in the long format. This document defines some of those previously unused bits as a class number.

Each class runs a separate copy of the Multilink mechanism, which means a separate sequence number space and a separate reassembly buffer. In the short sequence number format the header becomes begin bit, end bit, class number and sequence number, and in the long format the class number is four bits wide with the sequence number following in the same row.

Together with the ability to send packets without a multilink header, the memo says this provides four levels of suspension with 12-bit headers, probably sufficient for many practical applications, and sixteen levels with 24-bit headers, where only four of the six free bits are used, because sixteen levels should generally be more than sufficient.
sections.plainLanguage: The class number goes into bits that Multilink was not using. Every class is numbered separately and reassembled separately, so a high-priority fragment can be sent between the fragments of a low-priority packet without the receiver mixing the two up.

sections.title: Prefix Elision
sections.content:
For some applications every packet of a certain class has a common protocol identifier, or even more than one common prefix byte. In that case an optimisation is possible: the class number can be associated with a prefix of bytes which are removed from each packet before transmission and implicitly prepended to the reassembled packet after reception.

The memo notes a corner case. If only some of the packets to be transmitted at a certain priority level have the common prefix, it may still be possible to use the method by allocating two class numbers and associating only one of them with the prefix. That is the reason the memo allocated four of the unused bits in the long sequence number format to the class number instead of the three that should generally suffice.

Prefix elision is not a replacement for header compression or data compression. It allows implementations to compress away prefixes that are often not reachable by header or data compression methods.
sections.plainLanguage: When every packet of a class starts with the same bytes, those bytes can be left out of the fragments and added back when the packet is reassembled. The class number says which bytes to add back. This saves bytes that ordinary compression usually cannot reach.

sections.title: Negotiable Options
sections.content:
Multilink already defines three PPP LCP options: Multilink Maximum Received Reconstructed Unit, Multilink Short Sequence Number Header Format, and Endpoint Discriminator. This document defines two more, the Multilink Header Format option and the Prefix Elision option.

The Multilink Header Format option has type 27 and a length of 4. It carries a code and the number of suspendable classes. The option tells the peer that the implementation wishes to receive fragments in the format given by the code, with that many suspendable classes. When the option is negotiated, the accepting implementation must either transmit all subsequent multilink packets on all links of the bundle with the header format given, or Configure-Nak or Configure-Reject the option; an implementation may continue to send packets outside multilink in any case. A system offering the option on a link intended to join an existing bundle must offer the same option value that was previously negotiated for the bundle, or none if none was negotiated before.

Two code values are defined here: code 2 for the long sequence number fragment format with classes, and code 6 for the short sequence number fragment format with classes. The option must not occur more than once in a Configure-Request or Configure-Ack, and if it is present the Short Sequence Number Header Format option must not also be present. If neither this option nor the Short Sequence Number Header Format option is present but an MRRU option is, then by default long sequence number multilink headers with class 0 only are used, which is the same as code 2 with one suspendable class. An instance of the Short Sequence Number Header Format option is equivalent to this option with code 6 and one suspendable class.

The number of suspendable classes bounds the class numbers: only class numbers numerically lower than the limit can be used for suspendable classes. An implementation may negotiate a smaller number than the packet format allows, to limit the reassembly buffer space it needs. Implementations should at least support the value 4 for the short sequence number fragment format and the value 8 for the long sequence number fragment format, unless configured differently. Bit combinations that would indicate class numbers outside the negotiated range may be used for other semantics if they are negotiated by other means outside the scope of the memo.

The Prefix Elision option has type 26. Apart from the type and length octets common to all LCP options, it holds a sequence of zero or more sequences made of a single octet class number, a single octet giving the length of the prefix for that class, and the octets of that prefix. The option tells the peer that the implementation expects to receive, in each of the given classes, only packets with a certain prefix, and that this prefix is not to be sent as part of the information in the fragments of that class. By default the common prefix is empty for all classes. When the option is negotiated, the accepting implementation must either transmit all subsequent multilink packets of each of the given classes with the given prefix removed from the start of the packet, or Configure-Nak or Configure-Reject the option. If none of the formats with classes has been negotiated, class number 0 may be used to indicate a common prefix for all packets sent within multilink fragments.

The option must not occur more than once in a Configure-Request or Configure-Nak, and a system offering it on a link intended to join an existing multilink bundle must offer the same value previously negotiated for the bundle, or none if none was negotiated before. An implementation note adds that the sense of this option is an indication from the receiver to the sender about the packets concerned, and that often only the senders have enough control over their use of classes to supply useful values. A receiver willing to accept prefix-elided packets should request the option with empty content, leaving the sender free to use Configure-Nak to propose the class to prefix mapping it wants.
sections.plainLanguage: Two options are added to the link negotiation. One tells the peer which header format to use and how many priority levels are allowed. The other tells the peer which bytes are common to every packet of a class so that they can be left out. The two ends must agree, and a new link joining a bundle must offer the same values the bundle already agreed on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says operation of this protocol is believed to be no more and no less secure than operation of the PPP multilink protocol of RFC 1990. It sets out no other security requirements, and no separate threat analysis, because the change is confined to how fragments are labelled and numbered rather than to how they are protected.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says the scheme is exactly as secure as plain PPP Multilink, and adds nothing further.

Four with 12-bit headers, sixteen with 24-bit headers

viz.caption: THE FIVE IDEAS OF THE EXTENSION

items.title: Class number
items.text: Bits that the multilink header left unused now carry a class number.

items.title: Separate numbering
items.text: Each class has its own sequence number space, so classes do not mix.

items.title: Separate reassembly
items.text: Each class has its own reassembly buffer, so a fragment can be held while another class is sent.

items.title: Packets with no header
items.text: Traffic can still be sent with no multilink header, which adds one more level.

items.title: Prefix elision
items.text: Bytes common to a class can be left out of the fragments and restored on arrival.

viz.caption: OPTION TYPES AND HEADER FORMAT CODES

items.label: Prefix Elision option
items.desc: LCP option type 26. Carries a class number, a prefix length and the prefix octets for each class.

items.label: Multilink Header Format option
items.desc: LCP option type 27, length 4. Carries a format code and the number of suspendable classes.

items.label: Long sequence number with classes
items.desc: Code 2 of the Multilink Header Format option: the long sequence number fragment format with classes.

items.label: Short sequence number with classes
items.desc: Code 6 of the Multilink Header Format option: the short sequence number fragment format with classes.
